matches.gold_text: Proposals must be submitted by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025.
The program administrator(s) must develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep for Track A and/or Track B; ESD will award up to two contracts.
For Track A, the administrator must develop a targeted outreach and recruitment strategy for low-income students.
For Track A, the administrator must provide participant stipends and wrap-around supports including mentorships and career coaches with industry expertise.
The Track A curriculum should consist of online AI courses developed with input from leading researchers and industry experts, with mentorship opportunities and real-world machine learning projects.
For Track B, the administrator must deliver an industry-informed, comprehensive AI technology training program for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment and connect them to AI jobs.
The Track B program should consist of online AI courses with curriculum that incorporates industry input on technical skills and learning milestones.
The program should serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority given to applicants that serve more than 400 participants.
Over 50% of program participants should be low-income.
The majority of program graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.
Applicants must be organizations with a strong track record in workforce development in AI or similar fields.
If applicants form a team, one organization must be the lead for the proposed programming.

Applicants must have experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.
Proposed budgets may not exceed $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period, or they will not be considered.
The program operating period funded by ESD is up to 18 months.
Applicants must provide their own budget with associated justification.
Indirect costs are not allowable under this grant and must not be included in the budget.
The extent of any cost matching should be indicated in the budget template.
Awarded applicants must track and record information relevant to the success of the grant, with data points determined during contract negotiation.

For Track A, the administrator must help students secure paid internships.
For Track A, the administrator must create a program application and evaluation process and conduct needs assessments to identify and address student barriers to success.
For Track A, the administrator should propose whether training runs during the academic year or as summer courses, aligned with employer internship hiring cycles.

checklist.fact: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD) through its Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD), created after Governor Hochul's April 2022 announcement of $350 million for workforce development.

The need is that AI-related jobs often require specialized education and training out of reach for low-income individuals, creating a risk that AI progress will disproportionately benefit those already privileged and leave underrepresented communities behind.

AI Prep is an applied training program with two tracks: Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) for low-income matriculating undergraduates seeking paid internships, and Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs) for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment via accelerated training or bootcamp.
OSWD seeks to award contracts to up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep for Track A and/or Track B.
Funding is up to $2M per track (up to $4M total) for an initial term of up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need, and availability of funds.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the contract period will not be considered, and indirect costs are not allowable.
Program objectives require serving a minimum of 250 participants (priority for those serving more than 400), with over 50% low-income participants.
Most graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.

Applicants may be non-profit or for-profit and must have experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.
Proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, uploaded to a designated Dropbox; late proposals will not be accepted.
The anticipated schedule is: winner announced November 14, 2025, and contract start January 1, 2026.
Appendix A (ESD IT Security Standard Brief), Appendix B (Diversity Practices Questionnaire) and Schedule A (standard ESD contract terms) are referenced but not included in the RFP PDF.

specificity.reason: Roles, forms, insurance and data points are named concretely, but curriculum content, cohort sizes, stipend levels, employers and the academic-year vs summer decision are deferred to 'stated in the proposal'.

component_records.title: Program design, curriculum and employer-informed content
component_records.description: We develop the curriculum for and administer the AI Prep program across Track A and Track B as a single integrated program office, with one curriculum architecture serving both tracks and a named program director accountable for administering both (R005). The curriculum is industry-informed and built with input from leading researchers and industry experts, delivered as online AI courses with mentorship and real-world machine learning projects (R014, R019). It is designed to be immersive and deliverable part-time or full-time (R027), and we state in the proposal whether training runs during the academic year or in summer to align with employer internship hiring cycles. Employer partners review content each cohort so training stays aligned to hiring demand, and we state the credentials participants receive on completion, where applicable (R031).

component_records.title: Track A: AI Prep 4 Internships delivery
component_records.description: For Track A we deliver a comprehensive AI technology training program for low-income matriculating undergraduates aimed at paid internships at leading tech companies (R006, R009), tailored specifically to placements with leading New York State technology companies (R021). The program creates a direct education-to-AI-industry pathway and builds a talent pipeline for AI employers (R010), and internships are structured so students apply newly acquired AI skills to real work and build networks that lead to full-time roles (R022). We help students secure paid internships (R017) and report placement rates by low-income status.

component_records.title: Track B: AI Prep 4 Jobs delivery
component_records.description: For Track B we deliver an accelerated training or bootcamp that serves as an alternative to traditional degree programs, connecting low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment to AI jobs (R007). The program provides full-time job connection support in an AI-related field (R032) and professional development support throughout training (R030), with skill-attainment metrics measured during training (R029). We state the credentials expected on completion where applicable (R031) and report full-time placement rates by low-income status.

component_records.title: Outreach, recruitment, application and needs assessment
component_records.description: We run a targeted outreach and recruitment strategy for low-income students and New Yorkers underrepresented in tech who cannot reasonably access training on their own (R011, R008), working through community organizations, colleges and public workforce channels. We operate a program application and evaluation process (R012) with a published rubric, and conduct needs assessments to identify and address each participant's barriers to success (R013), feeding results into support plans. We state our proposed definition of low-income and our recruitment targeting in the proposal (R092), and we propose an alternative Pell Grant eligibility definition with justification where it better fits our population (R055).

component_records.title: Participant supports: stipends, mentors, coaches and professional development
component_records.description: We pay participant stipends and provide wrap-around supports including mentorships and career coaches with industry expertise (R016), with the stipend level and support package stated in the proposal and priced in the budget. Professional development runs throughout training (R030) and success coaching is available part-time or full-time depending on the participant's schedule. Supports are sized to the cohort model we propose and are reported as part of the program's completion metrics.

component_records.title: Employer partnerships and placement services
component_records.description: We cultivate and maintain relationships with leading industry employers to inform training content and generate paid internship opportunities (R018), and we help students secure paid internships (R017) and full-time AI-related jobs (R032). Placement staff coordinate directly with individual employers on role scoping, candidate matching and post-placement support, and we secure letters from partner employers committing to paid internships or full-time employment for graduates. We target the RFP's outcome expectations: a majority of graduates placed in AI or a closely related field, with at least 250 participants served and priority given to proposals exceeding 400 (R038, R041).

component_records.title: Program administration, scheduling and skill measurement
component_records.description: We deliver and manage the AI training program end to end (R015), running an immersive schedule available part-time or full-time (R027) with cohort sizes and training duration stated in the proposal. We measure participant skill attainment during training through defined evaluation metrics (R029) and report results to ESD alongside completion data. A program director owns the monthly delivery plan from planning through first-cohort internship or job completion, and we describe how AI Prep funding expands our existing similar programming, how many additional participants it lets us serve, and how we maintain or enhance quality (R086, R087, R088).

component_records.title: Data capture, performance metrics and reporting
component_records.description: We stand up a participant data system that captures and tracks the data points ESD specifies, with the exact list fixed at contract negotiation, including at minimum the number of applicants and the percentage that are low-income (R058). It tracks participants who enroll and the low-income percentage (R059), participants who complete and the low-income percentage (R060), the paid internship placement rate including low-income share (R061), the full-time job placement rate including low-income share (R062), participating colleges and universities (R063), and participating employer partners (R064). We commit to annual performance estimates against total participants served, low-income completion percentage and placement rate, justified by historical experience and partner commitments (R096), and we describe how we currently measure and report program success (R095).

component_records.title: Budget, pricing and cost justification
component_records.description: We submit a line-by-line price proposal of fees to accomplish the scope (R097), with Personnel Services costs broken out by job title, name where known, hourly or annual rate, fringe rate, percentage of time and cost to contract (R098), and Other Than Personnel Services costs on separate lines showing cost to contract and quantity (R099). The budget is mapped to the program duration (R049) and includes staff salary and benefits (R050), wraparound supports and the proposed participant stipend level (R051), and other program costs such as curriculum development, marketing and events (R052). Indirect costs are excluded entirely (R053), the extent of cost matching is indicated in the budget template (R054), and we provide our own budget with a full justification (R047). Total pricing stays within the $2M per track / $4M both-track ceiling (R034) for an initial term of up to 18 months (R035).

component_records.title: MWBE, SDVOB and diversity participation program
component_records.description: We build a subcontracting plan that meets ESD's 30 percent MWBE goal (R186) and 6 percent SDVOB goal, documenting good faith efforts to give MWBEs meaningful subcontractor and supplier participation (R185) and to give SDVOBs meaningful participation (R216). We submit an MWBE Utilization Plan and an SDVOB Utilization Plan on Form OCSD-4 listing each firm, the work it will perform and estimated dollar amounts (R218), and we count only sums paid for a commercially useful function (R188), applying the 25 percent broker rule where an MWBE acts as broker (R189). We follow our SDVOB Utilization Plan (R226), report any post-award changes on a revised plan (R219), accept that failure to use SDVOBs as agreed is a material breach (R227), and meet the SDVOB goals with willful failure treated as breach (R245). items.text: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD), a New York State economic development corporation whose mission is to promote a growing state economy, encourage business investment and job creation, and support diverse local economies through loans, grants, tax credits, real estate development and marketing.

ESD's Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD) was created as part of Governor Hochul's April 2022 $350 million workforce development investment and is charged with aligning workforce efforts to employer needs and creating opportunities for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented workers in high-growth sectors.

ESD identifies AI as a high-growth sector and New York as a key AI hub (citing Cornell Tech and Empire AI), but states that rapid AI advancement risks widening economic inequality because many well-paying AI jobs require specialized education and technical training out of reach for lower-income individuals.

The program responds to tech recruiting practices that favor students at elite schools and those with personal connections to prominent technology companies, which AI Prep is intended to counter by training low-income New Yorkers in AI skills.

ESD currently has no in-house delivery capability for this training and is procuring up to two external qualified program administrators to develop curriculum and administer the program for Track A and/or Track B.

ESD seeks to award contracts to up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep, an applied AI training program with two tracks: Track A "AI Prep 4 Internships" for low-income matriculating undergraduates and Track B "AI Prep 4 Jobs" for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment.

For Track A, the administrator must deliver a comprehensive AI technology training program for low-income college students including paid internship placements, with outreach and recruitment, application and evaluation, needs assessments, industry-informed curriculum, stipends and wrap-around supports (mentors, career coaches), and employer relationships generating paid internships.

For Track B, the administrator must deliver an industry-informed AI training program (accelerated training or bootcamp as an alternative to degree programs) with outreach, online AI courses, assessment, part-time or full-time immersive schedule, stipends and success coaches, skill-attainment metrics, professional development, credentials where applicable, and full-time AI job placement support.

The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for applicants proposing to serve more than 400, and the majority of graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.
The contract term is up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need and availability of funds, and the anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026.

The curriculum should consist of online AI courses developed with input from leading researchers and industry experts, with mentorship and real-world machine learning projects, and the administrator must propose whether training runs during the academic year or in summer to align with employer internship hiring cycles.
Proposals are scored out of a maximum of 100 points by an ESD selection committee, allocated as Firm Qualifications 15, Experience 25, Project Plan 30, Cost of Services 20 and Diversity Practices 10.

The Project Plan (30 points) must include a monthly timeline from planning through first-cohort internship or job completion, proposed training duration, cohort size, stipend level and supports, and letters from partner employers committing to paid internships or full-time employment, plus 1-page resumes of key personnel.

Proposers must estimate annual performance against three metrics — total participants served annually, percentage of low-income participants completing the curriculum, and paid internship or full-time job placement rate — justified by historical experience or partner commitments.

Awarded administrators must track and report data including applicant, enrollment and completion counts with low-income percentages, internship and job placement rates, participating colleges and employer partners, with the exact list set during contract negotiation.
Questions must be submitted by email to AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov by August 29, 2025, with ESD responses posted as an Addendum by September 12, 2025, and proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025.
Interviews, if necessary, are scheduled for the first week of November 2025 and the successful respondent is to be announced November 14, 2025.
ESD reserves the right to conduct reference checks at its sole discretion, using information from references on quality of services, ability to perform and responsiveness to the client.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period will not be considered, and ESD will invest up to $2M per track (up to $4M total).

Indirect costs are not an allowable cost under this grant, and the budget must map to Staff Salary and Benefits, Wraparound Supports and Participant Stipend Level, and other program costs such as curriculum development, marketing and events.
There is no cost-match requirement, but applicants can receive additional scoring points for cost matching, which must be indicated in the budget template.

Applicants must be non-profit or for-profit entities with experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.

Proposals must be uploaded as a two-part folder structure (Administrative and Technical subfolders) to the Dropbox at https://www.dropbox.com/request/AIPrep; fax, hardcopy and email submissions are not accepted and late proposals will not be considered.

The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, requiring an MWBE Utilization Plan and an SDVOB Utilization Plan (Form OCSD-4) with documented good faith efforts, quarterly MWBE compliance reports and monthly SDVOB compliance reports.

The selected contractor must carry Commercial General Liability of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate, $1M Commercial Automobile, $1M Sexual Abuse and Molestation coverage, and statutory Workers' Compensation, Employer's Liability and Disability coverage, naming ESD as additional insured with a waiver of subrogation.

Appendix A "ESD IT Security Standard Brief" and Appendix B "Diversity Practices Questionnaire" are referenced in the RFP but their content is not included in the RFP text provided, so bidders must obtain them separately.
ESD requires the administrator to propose whether training runs during the academic year or in summer to align with employer internship hiring cycles.
ESD is procuring up to two external program administrators to develop curriculum and administer the program for Track A and/or Track B.
Track A is aimed at low-income matriculating undergraduates and must include paid internship placements.
Track B must serve low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment through an accelerated training or bootcamp alternative to degree programs.
The program must serve New Yorkers currently underrepresented in the tech industry who cannot reasonably access training on their own.
The administrator must provide participant stipends and wrap-around supports including mentorships and career coaches with industry expertise.

The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for proposals to serve more than 400, and the majority of graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.
The contract term is up to 18 months with an anticipated start date of January 1, 2026.

Awarded administrators must track applicant, enrollment and completion counts with low-income percentages, internship and job placement rates, and participating colleges and employer partners, with the exact list set during contract negotiation.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period will not be considered, and indirect costs are not allowable.
The restricted period runs until approval of the Contract, and the designated contacts are Julia Borukhov and Jordan Kaplan.

The selected contractor must carry Commercial General Liability of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate, $1M Commercial Automobile, $1M Sexual Abuse and Molestation, and statutory Workers' Compensation, Employer's Liability and Disability coverage, naming ESD as additional insured with a waiver of subrogation.
The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, with quarterly MWBE and monthly SDVOB compliance reporting.
Proposals must be uploaded as a two-part folder structure to the Dropbox at https://www.dropbox.com/request/AIPrep, and fax, hardcopy and email submissions are not accepted.

The bidder proposes both tracks under a single lead organization, with one contract covering both tracks within the $4M combined ceiling, and states in the proposal that single-track awards are also acceptable to it.

Low-income eligibility is defined by the bidder in the proposal using a documented income standard (federal poverty level or area median income) with verification by documentation or attestation, subject to ESD confirmation at negotiation.

The program is designed for a minimum of 250 participants per track with cohort sizes and training duration set by the bidder in the proposal, and the bidder targets more than 400 participants to earn priority consideration.
Stipends are paid during both training and internship periods, with the split between training delivery and stipends set by the bidder within the $2M per track cap and disclosed in the budget.
The contract is priced and staffed for the initial 18-month term only, with renewal or extension priced separately if exercised.
The January 1, 2026 start date and the October 1, 2025 submission deadline are treated as firm for planning purposes, with any change communicated by ESD addendum.

The full data-point list and reporting format will be fixed at contract negotiation; the bidder builds a configurable data system covering the minimum points named in the RFP plus reasonable additions.
The bidder's own line-item cost schedule format is used for the price proposal, since no prescribed template is provided.
The Diversity Practices Questionnaire (Appendix B) is obtained from ESD and completed as a form, with a short narrative only where the form requires explanation.

The ESD IT Security Standard Brief (Appendix A) is obtained from ESD and its controls are applied to the participant data system; the bidder assumes no additional certification beyond those controls is required.
The 30 percent MWBE and 6 percent SDVOB goals apply to total contract value, and the bidder commits to meeting them through named subcontractors rather than relying on a waiver.
Commercial Automobile and Sexual Abuse and Molestation coverage are carried as required even if the bidder judges them only conditionally applicable, to avoid a responsiveness challenge.

The bidder's proposal includes only the content the RFP requests, with resumes and employer letters treated as expressly requested items, resolving the tension between the completeness and no-extra-information instructions.

Training is scheduled to align with employer internship hiring cycles, with the bidder proposing the academic-year or summer model in the proposal and offering part-time and full-time immersive options.

Budget cap may not cover 250+ participants with stipends across both tracks. The RFP caps the award at $2M per track and $4M for both tracks over up to 18 months, and that money must cover curriculum development, staff, wrap-around supports and participant stipends. The RFP does not say what share must go to stipends or how many participants must be served, so the bidder cannot tell whether the cap is workable. If the stipend level and participant count the proposal commits to turn out to be unaffordable within the cap, the bidder either loses points on cost or absorbs the shortfall. A fixed ceiling with an undefined stipend share and an undefined participant count is the single largest price driver; the solution assumes a stipend split set by the bidder within the cap, which is an inference the RFP does not confirm.

Employer commitment letters and paid placements may not materialise. The proposal must include letters from partner employers committing to paid internships or full-time employment, and the program is judged on a majority of graduates being placed in AI or a closely related field. The bidder does not yet hold those commitments, and placement outcomes depend on employers outside its control. Missing letters cost points at submission; weak placement performance costs the contract later. Placement is a scored outcome and a stated success criterion, and the solution relies on securing letters from partner employers before the October 1, 2025 deadline, which is a commitment the bidder cannot guarantee.

MWBE 30% and SDVOB 6% goals with liquidated damages and monthly reporting. The contract carries a 30 percent MWBE and 6 percent SDVOB participation goal, with liquidated damages equal to the shortfall for willful failure, payment withholding until documentation is received, and quarterly MWBE plus monthly SDVOB compliance reports. The solution commits to meeting the goals through named subcontractors rather than a waiver, but the certified firms and their commercially useful functions are not yet secured, so the bidder could face damages or a non-responsibility finding. The goals are firm, the remedies are contractual, and the solution's commitment to meet them without a waiver depends on subcontractors the bidder has not yet contracted; the broker rule also limits how much MWBE spend counts.

Low-income and barriers-to-employment definitions left to the bidder. The RFP does not define low-income, barriers to employment, or the income threshold used for reporting, yet the program must serve a majority low-income participants and report low-income percentages at every stage. If ESD later applies a different definition than the bidder's, recruitment targets, eligibility screening and reported performance all shift, and the bidder may have to re-screen or re-recruit cohorts. The solution assumes the bidder's own documented income standard will be accepted subject to ESD confirmation at negotiation, but the RFP leaves the definition open and it drives both eligibility and the reported metrics.

Schedule conflict between academic-year/summer model and part-time or full-time delivery. The RFP asks the proposal to state whether training runs during the academic year or in summer to align with employer internship cycles, and separately requires an immersive schedule deliverable part-time or full-time. The solution promises both without resolving which model governs, so the proposal may read as non-responsive or the delivery model may not fit employer hiring cycles. The two requirements pull in different directions and the solution addresses them by offering both options, which does not settle the schedule ESD will score or the internship timing employers will commit to.

Appendix A IT Security Standard Brief not available before pricing the data system. Appendix A, the ESD IT Security Standard Brief, is referenced but not included in the RFP, and the solution assumes its controls can be applied to the participant data system with no further certification. If the brief requires controls the bidder has not priced, the data system needs unplanned rework or additional security spend inside a capped budget. The document is missing from the RFP and the solution's assumption that no certification beyond those controls is required is unverified; the participant data system holds sensitive income and personal data.

Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire missing, worth 10 scoring points. The Diversity Practices Questionnaire is a required Technical Proposal item and carries 10 of the 100 scoring points, but the form itself is not in the RFP. If the bidder cannot obtain it in time, or guesses at its content, it risks losing the full 10 points or being found non-responsive for omitting a required item. The form is referenced but absent, and the solution assumes it will be obtained from ESD and completed as a form; the 10-point weight makes the omission material to the score.

Schedule A and Schedule B contract terms not reviewed before submission. Schedule A (standard contract requirements) and Schedule B (MWBE requirements and procedures) are referenced but not included in the RFP, and the bidder must accept them and raise any concerns with the Administrative Proposal. Accepting unseen terms risks committing to obligations, insurance or liability the bidder has not priced, and raising concerns late waives objections. Both schedules are missing from the RFP, the solution commits to accepting Schedule A and Schedule B, and the RFP sets no deadline for raising concerns, so the bidder cannot tell when objections become time-barred.

Participant data points and reporting format fixed only at contract negotiation. The RFP leaves the full data-point list and reporting format to contract negotiation, while the solution commits to a configurable data system covering the named minimums. If ESD adds data points or reporting frequency after award, the bidder absorbs unplanned system build and analyst time inside a capped budget. The requirement explicitly defers the list to negotiation and the solution's assumption of a configurable system is an inference; the reporting obligation runs for the whole 18-month term.

18-month term with undefined renewal and a January 1, 2026 start. The contract runs up to 18 months from an anticipated January 1, 2026 start, with renewal or extension left open as to number, maximum duration and criteria. The solution prices and staffs only the initial term, so if ESD extends, the bidder must re-price staff and stipends, and if the start slips, the cohort and internship calendar compresses against the term. The renewal terms are undefined and the start date is only anticipated; the solution assumes the January 1, 2026 start is firm and prices the initial term only.

Administrative forms and certifications are externally linked and easy to miss. The Administrative Proposal requires a long list of forms in a fixed order, including the Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, 139-j/139-k forms, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire, Iran Divestment Act Statement, EO 16 and 177 certifications, ST-220-CA, W-9 and OCSD-1, most of which are provided only by external link. A missing or out-of-order item can result in rejection, and the RFP does not say whether omissions can be cured after submission. The forms are numerous, externally hosted and must be submitted in a specified order, and the RFP states failure may result in rejection without saying whether it is curable.

Technical Proposal scope conflict: completeness versus no extra information. The RFP tells respondents to provide all requested information clearly and concisely, and separately forbids including any information beyond what is specifically requested. The solution resolves this by treating resumes and employer letters as expressly requested, but other supporting material the bidder might add (case studies, sample curricula, references) could be read as a violation and cost points or responsiveness. The two instructions conflict and the RFP does not say whether supporting materials are permitted; the solution's resolution is an inference rather than a stated rule.
